title: No rate limit, no mercy
brief: 17:30. Monitoring shows the sign in endpoint doing forty thousand requests in ten minutes, from a handful of addresses. Nothing is slowing them down.
role: Platform engineer, reviewing a change on the Veltrix engineering team
insight: The endpoint answers as fast as it is asked, forever, so guessing is free.
teaches: Limit attempts per account and per source, and back off or lock after failures
Alert on spikes of failed sign ins so a person notices
A vaguer error message helps, but it is not a limit; a CAPTCHA on one client is not a limit either

value.title: Sign in endpoint
value.intro: Replay what the attacker did, against staging. Start with one careful guess, then a burst.

attempts.label: Sign in once, with a wrong password
Try 5,000 passwords on one account in a minute
attempts.request: for pw in wordlist[0..5000]: POST /v1/login  email=megan@customer.test
attempts.response:
4,999 x HTTP 401
1 x HTTP 200  (password: "Summer2026!")

Signed in as Megan after 96 seconds. Nothing slowed down, locked, or alerted.
attempts.fixedResponse:
3 x HTTP 401
47 x HTTP 429  Too many attempts. Try again in 15 minutes.
Account locked for 15 minutes. Alert raised: "1,200 failed sign ins for one account".

attempts.label: Try one leaked password across 2,000 accounts
attempts.request: for email in leaked_list[0..2000]: POST /v1/login  password="Summer2026!"
attempts.response:
2,000 requests, 31 x HTTP 200

31 accounts opened with one password. Nothing counted them.
attempts.fixedResponse:
60 x HTTP 401, then HTTP 429 for that source address.
Alert raised: "1 address, 60 different accounts".

fix.prompt: Pick every change that limits the guessing, and makes sure a person is told when it happens.

options.label: Rate limit per account and per source address
code: +   rate_limit: 5 per minute per account, 30 per minute per address
options.why: Guessing at speed stops working, both against one account and across many.

options.label: Back off and temporarily lock after repeated failures, and add a second factor for risky sign ins
code: +   step_up: mfa when new device or country
options.why: A guessed password alone is no longer enough to get in.

options.label: Alert on spikes of failed sign ins, per account and per address
options.why: A person finds out in minutes, not after the customers complain.

options.label: Make the error message vaguer
options.why: Helps a little against knowing which emails exist. It does nothing to the speed of guessing.

options.label: Add a CAPTCHA to the website login form
options.why: The attacker uses the API directly and never sees the form.

outcome.label: Read the vulnerable code first
outcome.what: Reading the code before attacking it tells you where to look, and why it fails.
outcome.ideal: reads the code under review before trying to break it.

outcome.label: Tried normal use first
outcome.what: Knowing what a good request looks like is how you spot a bad one.
outcome.ideal: establishes normal behaviour before testing the abnormal.

outcome.label: Checked normal use still works
outcome.what: A fix that breaks real users gets reverted, and the bug comes back.
outcome.ideal: tests that the fix did not break normal use.

exploit.objective: Reproduce the bug: read the Code tab, then use the Exploit tab on staging.
exploit.insight: The endpoint answers as fast as it is asked, forever, so guessing is free.

label: Send this request: it breaks it
Open the Exploit tab

hint.text: Open the Workbench. Read the code, try normal use on the Exploit tab, then send the request that breaks it.

outcome.label: Reproduced the bug
outcome.what: With no limit, no lockout and no alert, one account fell to a wordlist in 96 seconds, and a single leaked password opened 31 accounts. Nothing noticed either.
outcome.ideal: proves a bug is real before fixing it.

card.title: Guessing was free
body: With no limit, no lockout and no alert, one account fell to a wordlist in 96 seconds, and a single leaked password opened 31 accounts. Nothing noticed either.
This is credential stuffing: not clever, just unmetered.
card.ideal: reproduces a bug first, so the fix can be proved to work.

fix.objective: Fix it: pick the changes on the Fix tab that close the hole for good, then apply the patch.

label: Picked everything that fixes it? Apply the patch
Pick every change that fixes the cause
Open the Fix tab

hint.text: Pick every change that removes the cause. Avoid changes an attacker can walk around, and ones that do not touch the problem. Then Apply the patch.

outcome.label: Applied a real fix
outcome.what: Rate limits per account and per address stop both the burst and the spray. Backoff and a second factor mean a guessed password is not enough, and an alert means a person knows within minutes.
outcome.ideal: fixes the cause, not the symptom.

card.title: Slow, locked, and noticed
body: Rate limits per account and per address stop both the burst and the spray. Backoff and a second factor mean a guessed password is not enough, and an alert means a person knows within minutes.
Every layer is cheap. Together they turn free guessing into a losing bet.
card.ideal: fixes the cause with the standard control, and adds defence in depth.

outcome.label: Applied a fix that can be bypassed
outcome.what: A vaguer message and a CAPTCHA on the website change how the front door looks. The API is still open, and attackers use the API. Neither slows a script, and neither tells anyone it is happening.
outcome.ideal: fixes the cause instead of blocking one payload or hiding the symptom.

card.title: The wrong layer
body: A vaguer message and a CAPTCHA on the website change how the front door looks. The API is still open, and attackers use the API. Neither slows a script, and neither tells anyone it is happening.
Limit the attempts, and alert on them.
card.ideal: fixes the cause, and knows why a blocklist or a hidden field is not a fix.

outcome.label: Applied a patch that was not enough
outcome.what: The patch missed part of the fix, or added a change that does not address the problem.

card.title: Not enough
body: The patch missed something that has to change, or included a change that does nothing for this bug. Open the Fix tab to see which options were right, missed, or wrong, and why.
A partial fix is the most dangerous kind: everyone assumes it is closed.

verify.objective: Prove it: re-run the exploit on the Exploit tab, then check normal use still works.

label: Send the exploit again: it should be blocked
Open the Exploit tab

hint.text: On the Exploit tab, send the exploit again. It should be blocked. Then send the normal request to check nothing broke.

outcome.label: Proved the exploit is blocked
outcome.what: The same request that worked before now fails, and normal use still works.
outcome.ideal: verifies a fix by re-running the exploit.

card.title: Fixed, and proved
body: You re-ran the exact request that broke it, and it is blocked. A fix you have not tested against the exploit is a hope, not a fix.
Add the exploit as an automated test so nobody can quietly bring the bug back.
card.ideal: turns the exploit into a regression test.

outcome.label: The exploit still works
outcome.what: The patch did not close the hole. The same kind of request still gets through.
outcome.ideal: never ships a fix without re-running the exploit.

card.title: Still open
body: The exploit still works after your patch. This is what happens when a fix blocks one payload, or hides a symptom, instead of removing the cause.
Go back over the Fix tab: it shows which options were right, and why the others fail.
card.ideal: verifies with the exploit before calling it fixed.
